short: SPI1 (PU.1), SPIB and SPIC are the class III branch of the ETS family. They read the same GGA(A/T) core as other ETS proteins but demand a purine-rich 5' flank, giving the hematopoietic PU-box AAAGAGGAAGTG - the one ETS subfamily that a scan can usually tell apart from the rest. SPI1 is required for macrophage, neutrophil, dendritic cell and B-cell development; SPIB acts in B cells and plasmacytoid dendritic cells; SPIC specifies red pulp macrophages. PU.1 also nucleates the ETS-IRF composite element (EICE), GGAAGTGAAAC, by recruiting IRF4 or IRF8 to DNA it has already bound. Reduced PU.1 dosage causes acute myeloid leukemia in mice, and SPI1 fusions occur in high-risk pediatric T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
long:
## The factors

Three human genes - SPI1 (PU.1, Spi-1), SPIB (Spi-B) and SPIC (Spi-C) - form the SPI subfamily.
Each carries one ETS domain of about 85 residues with the family's winged helix-turn-helix fold and
binds DNA as a monomer; outside the domain they have acidic and glutamine-rich activation regions
and, in PU.1, a PEST region whose Ser148 must be phosphorylated for cooperative assembly with IRF
partners. Systematic profiling of all human and mouse ETS proteins puts these three in their own
class (class III), the most sequence-distinct group in the family; a tyrosine that sets specificity
at the position immediately 3' of the core in other ETS proteins is replaced by asparagine here.
Expression is hematopoietic and essentially non-overlapping with the rest of the family: SPI1 in
myeloid cells, macrophages, dendritic cells, microglia and B cells; SPIB in B cells and
plasmacytoid dendritic cells; SPIC narrowly in red pulp macrophages and related tissue macrophages.
The first crystal structure of any ETS domain on DNA was PU.1's, which established the
loop-helix-loop mode of DNA contact for the whole family.

## The motif

The site is usually written AAAGAGGAAGTG, and the models grouped here agree on AAAGAGGAAGT. The
invariant part is the same GGA(A/T) core all ETS proteins read, contacted by two invariant
arginines in recognition helix H3 that hydrogen-bond the two guanines, with a wing lysine 5' of the
core and a turn lysine on the opposite strand 3' of it. What sets this family apart is the 5' flank.
Class I ETS proteins prefer ACC immediately 5' of GGA; the SPI proteins prefer purines - AGA, with
a marked preference for G two bases 5' of the core - and tolerate a run of As further out. Because
that difference spans three or four positions rather than one, class III motifs are the only ETS
subfamily that a sequence scan separates from the rest with any reliability. Within the family,
SPI1, SPIB and SPIC are not separable: their models are near-identical, and the Vierstra archetype
that represents them is named for two of the three factors at once (AC0642:SPIB/SPI). Note that
the published PU.1 site contains no CpG, so unlike the class I CCGGAAGT it is insensitive to
CpG methylation. The composite EICE, GGAAGTGAAAC, is a PU.1 site fused to an IRF half-site and is
captured by only one model in this family - the CIS-BP entry M07944, whose consensus AAAGAGGAAGTGAAA
runs from the PU.1 site into the IRF half-site.

## Where it acts

PU.1 sites are found at myeloid and B-lineage promoters and, more heavily, at the enhancers that
define those lineages; the classic example is the macrophage colony-stimulating factor receptor
(CSF1R) promoter, where PU.1 directs macrophage-specific expression. PU.1 behaves as a lineage
"pioneer" in the sense that its binding precedes and is required for much of the accessible
chromatin landscape of myeloid cells, so its motif is enriched in macrophage and B-cell DNase and
ATAC footprints far more than in other cell types. Two named composite elements dominate its
cooperative biology. The EICE (ETS-IRF composite element, GGAAGTGAAAC) was defined at
immunoglobulin light-chain enhancers, where DNA-bound and Ser148-phosphorylated PU.1 recruits IRF4
(originally Pip) or IRF8, raising IRF affinity 20- to 40-fold; the crystal structure of the
PU.1/IRF4/DNA complex shows the DNA bent into an S shape that juxtaposes the two domains across the
central minor groove, and explains why IRF1 and IRF2 are anti-cooperative with PU.1 at the same
element. PU.1 sites also cluster with CEBP, RUNX and GATA sites in myeloid enhancers.

## Biology and disease

Spi1-null mice lack macrophages, neutrophils and B cells and have severely disrupted myeloid and
lymphoid development, the most striking single-gene hematopoietic phenotype among the ETS family.
Dosage matters as much as presence: reducing PU.1 expression to roughly a fifth of normal in mice
causes acute myeloid leukemia, placing SPI1 among the transcription factors whose partial loss is
leukemogenic. SPIC is required for red pulp macrophage development and splenic iron recycling.
In human disease, recurrent SPI1 fusions (STMN1-SPI1, TCF7-SPI1) define a high-risk subgroup of
pediatric T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, and PU.1 activity is a recurring theme in myeloid
leukemia biology more broadly.

## Reading a hit

A purine-rich AAAGAGGAAGTG match is one of the few ETS hits that genuinely localizes the signal to
a subfamily - but only to the subfamily. SPI1, SPIB and SPIC cannot be told apart by sequence, and
the atlas's representative model for this family is itself named for two factors. The distinction
from class I ETS is real but not absolute: degenerate members of this family, such as HOCOMOCO's
short SPI1.H14CORE.1.S.B model whose consensus is only GGAAGT, will match generic ETS sites, and
the GGAA core alone is expected millions of times per strand in a 3.1-Gb genome. Cell type carries
much of the inference: outside myeloid, B-lineage or microglial contexts a PU-box match is far more
likely to be a chance GGAA than a bound PU.1 site. Two caveats specific to this family: only one of its
twelve models (CIS-BP M07944, AAAGAGGAAGTGAAA) reaches into the IRF half-site, so scanning with the
rest will find the PU.1 half of an EICE without flagging the composite - look explicitly for GTGAAAC
a few bases 3' of the core; and the JASPAR
SPIB model (MA0081.3) is stored on the reverse strand as CACTTCCTCTT, the same site as AAGAGGAAGTG.
caveats:
This is one of the few ETS subfamilies a scan can separate from the others, because
its purine-rich 5' flank differs over three or four positions rather than one. It cannot separate
its own members: SPI1, SPIB and SPIC share one motif, and the atlas representative is a Vierstra
archetype named for two of them. Expression usually decides - SPIC is confined to red pulp
macrophages, SPIB to B cells and plasmacytoid dendritic cells - so a PU-box hit outside a
hematopoietic context deserves scepticism. The family is small (12 models) and includes short,
degenerate entries that behave like a generic ETS site. Only one of the twelve models reaches into the IRF half-site of
the EICE composite, so a scan will usually register the PU.1 half-site and miss the element that
gives it specificity.
